query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thin refractory high-entropy alloy interlayer (e.g., (CrFeTiTa)70W30) onto tungsten particles before embedding them into a copper matrix will reduce phase separation and void formation during consolidation, thereby enhancing interfacial bonding, mechanical durability, and thermal transport under irradiation compared to conventional spark-plasma sintering.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles or connected W regions within a continuous Cu matrix fabricated by conventional methods (e.g., spark-plasma sintering) that exhibit interfacial voids and phase separation.
generation.intervention: Apply a uniform, nanoscale coating of a refractory high-entropy alloy (such as (CrFeTiTa)70W30) on tungsten particles prior to embedding in the copper matrix.
generation.conditions: Composite consolidation performed via spark-plasma sintering at temperatures below the boiling point of Cu (<1000 °C) with subsequent exposure to thermal cycling and irradiation conditions typical of fusion-reactor joints.
generation.structural_mediator: The high-entropy alloy interlayer serves as a graded interface that minimizes interfacial energy differences and thermal expansion mismatches between tungsten and copper.
generation.mechanism: The interlayer improves wettability and chemical compatibility at the W–Cu interface, reducing void formation and phase separation during sintering. This graded interface stabilizes the microstructure under irradiation, preserving mechanical durability and thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to composites made by conventional spark-plasma sintering without the interlayer, the intervention is expected to produce W–Cu composites with significantly reduced void content, improved interfacial bonding, higher thermal conductivity, and retained mechanical durability under irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: W–Cu composites fabricated by spark-plasma sintering without a pre-deposited high-entropy alloy interlayer.
generation.boundary: Processing must be conducted at temperatures below copper’s boiling point during sintering, and the material must withstand thermal flux and irradiation levels encountered in fusion reactor joints.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal thickness and composition of the high-entropy alloy interlayer remain to be determined, as does its long-term microstructural and irradiation stability under operational fusion-reactor conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two batches of W–Cu composites under the same spark-plasma sintering conditions: one where W particles are pre-coated with a thin (CrFeTiTa)70W30 high-entropy alloy layer and one without any coating. Subject both batches to identical thermal cycling and irradiation tests that simulate fusion reactor joint conditions.
measurements: Void content and interfacial integrity via high-resolution microscopy and spectroscopy
Thermal conductivity tests before and after irradiation
Mechanical property evaluations (e.g., hardness, tensile strength, fatigue resistance)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the composites with the high-entropy alloy interlayer do not show statistically significant improvements in reduced void content, enhanced interfacial bonding, better thermal conductivity, and superior mechanical performance under irradiation compared to the baseline composites, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractNuclear fusion is a promising energy source. The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor aims to study the feasibility of tokamak-type reactors and test technologies and materials for commercial use. One major challenge is developing materials for the reactor’s divertor, which supports high thermal flux. Tungsten was chosen as the plasma-facing material, while a CuCrZr alloy will be used in the cooling pipes. However, the gradient between the working temperatures of these materials requires the use of a thermal barrier interlayer between them. To this end, refractory high-entropy (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys were prepared by mechanical alloying and sintering, and their thermal and irradiation resistance was evaluated. Both alloys showed phase growth after annealing at 1100 °C for 8 days, being more pronounced for higher temperatures (1300 °C and 1500 °C). The VFeTiTaW alloy presented greater phase growth, suggesting lower microstructural stability, however, no new phases were formed.
